title: Chapter 104 — The Fossil Whale
paragraphs: From his mighty bulk, the whale affords a most fitting theme on which to enlarge, amplify, and generally expand. Would you could not compress him. By rights he should only be treated in the largest format. Not to repeat his furlongs from blowhole to tail and the yards he measures around the waist — only think of the gigantic windings of his intestines, where they lie in him like great cables and hawsers coiled away in the lowest deck of a warship.

Since I have undertaken to grapple with this Leviathan, it is my duty to be exhaustively thorough in the enterprise — not overlooking the minutest seeds of his blood and spinning him out to the uttermost coil of his bowels. Having already described him in most of his present physical and anatomical peculiarities, it now remains to magnify him from an archaeological, fossil, and pre-flood point of view. Applied to any other creature than the Leviathan — to an ant or a flea — such grand terms might justly be deemed unwarrantably inflated. But when Leviathan is the text, the case is different. I am glad to stagger to this task under the weightiest words of the dictionary. And here let it be said that whenever it has been convenient to consult one in the course of these essays, I have invariably used a huge quarto edition of Johnson, expressly purchased for that purpose — because that famous lexicographer's uncommon personal bulk better fitted him to compile a lexicon to be used by a whale author like me.

One often hears of writers that rise and swell with their subject, though it may seem an ordinary one. How, then, with me, writing of this Leviathan? Unconsciously my handwriting expands into billboard capitals. Give me a condor's quill! Give me Vesuvius' crater for an inkstand! Friends, hold my arms! For in the mere act of putting pen to my thoughts of this Leviathan, they weary me and make me faint with their outreaching sweep, as if to include the whole circle of the sciences, and all the generations of whales and men and mastodons, past, present, and to come, with all the revolving panoramas of empire on earth and throughout the whole universe, not excluding its suburbs. Such, and so magnifying, is the virtue of a large and liberal theme! We expand to its bulk. To produce a mighty book, you must choose a mighty theme. No great and enduring volume can ever be written on the flea, though many there be who have tried it.

Before entering upon the subject of fossil whales, I present my credentials as a geologist by stating that in my miscellaneous time I have been a stone-mason, and also a great digger of ditches, canals, and wells, wine-vaults, cellars, and cisterns of all sorts. Likewise, as a preliminary, I wish to remind the reader that while in the earlier geological layers there are found fossils of monsters now almost completely extinct, the later relics discovered in what are called the Tertiary formations seem the connecting links between the ancient creatures and those whose remote descendants are said to have entered the Ark. All the fossil whales hitherto discovered belong to the Tertiary period, which is the last before the surface formations. And though none of them precisely match any known species of the present time, they are yet sufficiently similar in general respects to justify their being ranked as cetacean fossils.

Detached broken fossils of pre-human whales — fragments of their bones and skeletons — have within the past thirty years, at various intervals, been found at the base of the Alps, in Lombardy, in France, in England, in Scotland, and in the states of Louisiana, Mississippi, and Alabama. Among the more curious of such remains is part of a skull which in 1779 was dug up in the Rue Dauphine in Paris, a short street opening almost directly upon the palace of the Tuileries — and bones unearthed in excavating the great docks of Antwerp in Napoleon's time. Cuvier pronounced these fragments to have belonged to some utterly unknown Leviathanic species.

But by far the most wonderful of all cetacean relics was the almost complete vast skeleton of an extinct monster, found in 1842 on the plantation of Judge Creagh in Alabama. The awestruck credulous slaves in the vicinity took it for the bones of one of the fallen angels. The Alabama doctors declared it a huge reptile and bestowed upon it the name of Basilosaurus. But some specimen bones of it being taken across the sea to Owen, the English anatomist, it turned out that this alleged reptile was a whale, though of a vanished species. A significant illustration of the fact, again and again repeated in this book, that the skeleton of the whale furnishes but little clue to the shape of his fully living body. So Owen rechristened the monster Zeuglodon; and in his paper read before the London Geological Society, pronounced it, in substance, one of the most extraordinary creatures which the changes of the globe have wiped from existence.

When I stand among these mighty Leviathan skeletons, skulls, tusks, jaws, ribs, and vertebrae — all showing partial resemblances to the existing breeds of sea-monsters, but at the same time bearing similar likenesses to the destroyed ancient Leviathans, their incalculable elders — I am, by a flood, borne back to that wondrous period before time itself can be said to have begun, for time began with man. Here Saturn's gray chaos rolls over me, and I obtain dim, shuddering glimpses into those polar eternities, when wedged walls of ice pressed hard upon what are now the Tropics, and in all the 25,000 miles of this world's circumference, not an inhabitable hand's breadth of land was visible. Then the whole world was the whale's, and, king of creation, he left his wake along the present lines of the Andes and the Himalayas. Who can show a pedigree like Leviathan? Ahab's harpoon had shed older blood than the Pharaoh's. Methuselah seems a schoolboy. I look round to shake hands with Shem. I am horror-struck at this ancient, sourceless existence of the unspeakable terrors of the whale, which, having been before all time, must needs exist after all human ages are over.

But not alone has this Leviathan left his pre-human traces in the stereotype plates of nature, and in limestone and marl bequeathed his ancient form. Upon Egyptian tablets, whose antiquity seems to claim for them an almost fossil character, we find the unmistakable print of his fin. In an apartment of the great temple of Denderah, some fifty years ago, there was discovered upon the granite ceiling a sculptured and painted star-map, abounding in centaurs, griffins, and dolphins, similar to the fantastical figures on the celestial globe of the moderns. Gliding among them, old Leviathan swam as of old — was there swimming in that star-map centuries before Solomon was cradled.
Nor must there be omitted another strange evidence of the antiquity of the whale, in his own actual bony reality, as set down by the venerable John Leo, the old Barbary traveler.

"Not far from the seaside, they have a Temple, the rafters and beams of which are made of whale-bones; for whales of a monstrous size are oftentimes cast up dead upon that shore. The common people imagine that by a secret power bestowed by God upon the Temple, no whale can pass it without immediate death. But the truth of the matter is that on either side of the Temple there are rocks that shoot two miles into the sea and wound the whales when they strike upon them. They keep a whale's rib of an incredible length for a miracle, which lying upon the ground with its curved part uppermost makes an arch, the top of which cannot be reached by a man upon a camel's back. This rib, says John Leo, is said to have lain there a hundred years before I saw it. Their historians affirm that a prophet who prophesied of Muhammad came from this Temple, and some do not hesitate to assert that the prophet Jonah was cast forth by the whale at the base of the Temple."
In this African Temple of the Whale I leave you, reader. And if you be a Nantucketer and a whaleman, you will silently worship there.
